title: Estimates vary
objectives: See the sampling distribution of the mean by simulation.
Compute the standard error $\sigma / \sqrt n$ and tell it from the spread of the data.

screens.title: A thousand analysts
screens.prose: Here are the 100 daily returns from the last lesson: $\mu = 0.10\%$, $\sigma = 1.00\%$. Samples A and B averaged 0.42% and −0.15%. Now 1,000 analysts each draw 10 days at random and average them.
screens.question: How will the 1,000 averages be spread?

options.text: Bunched around 0.10%, much tighter than the daily returns
Spread like the daily returns, from about −2% to 3%
options.why: You gave the averages the spread of single days. Averaging 10 days lets big ups and downs cancel.
You expected every average to hit $\mu$. Samples A and B already missed, by 0.32% and 0.25%.
You anchored on the first sample. Sample A is one draw; the others have no reason to follow it.

hints.text: Samples A and B missed $\mu$, but by less than a typical day moves. Why?
A single day can be −1.9% or 2.9%. An average of 10 rarely is.
Highs and lows inside a sample offset each other, so averages sit closer to the middle than single days do.

feedback.correct: Averages cancel some of the noise, so they bunch around $\mu$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what averaging does to a big up day and a big down day.

explain.text: A sample of 10 usually mixes up days with down days, so its average lands near the middle. We will check this by simulation next. Single days range over 4.8 percentage points; most averages of 10 will not.

screens.title: Run the analysts
screens.prose: Each trial draws 10 of the 100 days at random, with replacement, and records their average. Run 10, then 100, then 1,000 trials. The dashed lines are the exact shares in the long run.

params.xLabel: Average of 10 days drawn at random (%)

screens.question: Where is the histogram of averages centred?

options.text: Near 0, because ups and downs cancel
options.why: You expected the averages to cancel to nothing. They cancel towards the population mean, 0.10%, not towards 0.
Look at the tallest bars: they sit on either side of 0.1. Sample A was one high draw.

options.text: Nowhere in particular: it keeps moving
options.why: Run 1,000 trials. The shape settles on the dashed lines, which balance at 0.10%.

hints.text: Run 1,000 trials and find the tallest bars.
The tallest bar runs from 0 to 0.2.
The bar from 0 to 0.2 is the tallest, and the shape balances at 0.10%.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run 1,000 trials and look where the histogram balances.

explain.text: After 1,000 trials the average of the 1,000 averages is 0.095%, against $\mu = 0.10\%$. In the long run the centre is exactly $\mu$: $E[\bar X] = \mu$. Single samples miss both ways, but the misses cancel.

canvas.caption: 1,000 samples of 10 days: mean of the averages 0.095%, sd 0.312%

screens.title: The spread of the average
screens.prose: The histogram you built is the **sampling distribution** of $\bar X$: every value the average could take, with its chance. Its sd has a name, the **standard error**. From the last course, $\mathrm{Var}(\bar X) = \sigma^2 / n$.

params.xLabel: Average of 10 days drawn at random (%)

state.caption: The sampling distribution of $\bar X$ for $n = 10$

screens.question: With $\sigma = 1.00\%$ and $n = 10$, what is the standard error of $\bar X$?

hints.text: The standard error is the square root of $\mathrm{Var}(\bar X)$.
The histogram runs from about −0.6% to 0.8%. Its sd is well under 1%.
$\sqrt{\sigma^2 / n} = \sigma / \sqrt{n} = 1 / \sqrt{10}$.

feedback.correct: $1\% / \sqrt{10} \approx 0.316\%$, and the 1,000 simulated averages had sd 0.312%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the square root of $\sigma^2 / n$.

byKey.sigma: 1.00% is the sd of a single day. The average of 10 days is less spread out than one day.
byKey.over-n: You divided $\sigma$ by $n$. The variance divides by $n$, so the sd divides by $\sqrt n$.
byKey.variance: You typed 10% or so. Check the units: the standard error is $1\% / \sqrt{10}$, about a third of a percent.

explain.text: $\mathrm{SE}(\bar X) = \sigma / \sqrt{n} = 1\% / \sqrt{10} \approx 0.316\%$. Your 1,000 simulated averages had sd 0.312%, close to it. About two thirds of the averages land within 0.316% of $\mu$.

canvas.caption: From −0.2% to 0.4%, about one standard error either side of $\mu$: 66% of samples

screens.title: More days, less spread
screens.prose: The tall curve is the sampling distribution of $\bar X$ for $n$ days, from the central limit theorem. The dashed curve is a single day.
screens.question: Slide $n$ until the standard error is 0.20%.

hints.text: Read the caption as you slide: it shows $1\% / \sqrt{n}$.
You need $\sqrt{n} = 1 / 0.2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Watch the caption until it reads 0.200%.

byKey.over-n: At $n = 5$ the caption reads 0.447%. You divided by $n$; the sd divides by $\sqrt n$.
byKey.short: The caption is still above 0.200%. Keep adding days.
byKey.long: The caption has gone below 0.200%. You have added too many days.

explain.text: At $n = 25$ the curve has sd $1\% / 5 = 0.20\%$, a fifth of a single day's spread. Going from 4 days to 25 cut the error from 0.5% to 0.2%. The centre never moved: it stays at $\mu$.

screens.title: Halving the error
screens.prose: At $n = 25$ the standard error is 0.20%. Try other values of $n$ first.
screens.question: How many days give a standard error of 0.10%, half of that?

hints.text: Halving $1 / \sqrt{n}$ means doubling $\sqrt{n}$.
Slide to 50 and read the caption: is it 0.10%?
$\sqrt{n}$ goes from 5 to 10, so $n$ goes from 25 to 100.

feedback.correct: Four times the days for half the error.

byKey.double: At 50 days the error is $1 / \sqrt{50} \approx 0.141\%$. Doubling the data does not halve the error.
byKey.squared: You squared 25. Halving the error needs $\sqrt n$ doubled, so $n = 4 \times 25$.

explain.text: Halving the standard error needs $\sqrt n$ doubled, so four times the data. That is the square-root law. Precision is expensive: every extra decimal place costs a hundred times the days.

screens.title: A sample of one
screens.prose: Now slide $n$ all the way down to 1.
screens.question: At $n = 1$, what is the sampling distribution of $\bar X$?

options.text: The population of daily returns itself

options.why: You treated one day as the mean. A single day can be anything from −1.9% to 2.9%.

options.text: There is none: you cannot average one number
options.why: The average of one number is that number. Its distribution is the spread of single days.
You expected a small sample to add spread. With $n = 1$, $\sigma / \sqrt 1 = \sigma$: exactly a day's spread.

hints.text: What is the average of one day's return?
At $n = 1$ the two curves lie on top of each other.
$\bar X = X_1$, so its distribution is a single day's, with sd $\sigma / \sqrt 1 = \sigma$.

feedback.correct: One draw: the sampling distribution is the population.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. With one day, the average is just that day.

explain.text: With one day, $\bar X = X_1$, so its distribution is the population's and its sd is $\sigma$. That is the edge case. Every extra day narrows the curve from there.

screens.title: The spread of what?
screens.prose: Rachel has 25 daily returns from a new fund. Their mean is 0.12% and their sd is 1.5%. She writes: "Our mean is 0.12%, give or take 1.5%."
screens.question: What is the standard error of her mean?

options.why: You used the spread of the data. 1.5% is how far one day strays; the average of 25 strays much less.
You divided by $n = 25$. The sd of the mean divides by $\sqrt{25} = 5$.
You computed $s^2 / n = 2.25 / 25$, a variance. Take its square root.

hints.text: Is 1.5% the spread of single days or of the average?
The standard error row is the one asked for.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The spread of the mean is the spread of a day divided by $\sqrt n$.

byKey.sd: You used the spread of the data for the spread of the mean. One day strays by 1.5%; the average of 25 strays by $1.5\% / 5$.

explain.text: The sd of the data says how much one day moves: 1.5%. The standard error says how much the average moves from sample to sample: $1.5\% / \sqrt{25} = 0.3\%$. Rachel should write "0.12%, give or take 0.3%".

screens.title: Why $\sqrt n$
screens.prose: Each of the $n$ draws $X_i$ has variance $\sigma^2$, and the draws are independent. Derive the variance of their average.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\mathrm{Var}(\bar X) = \mathrm{Var}\left(\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)$: the definition of $\bar X$
$= \tfrac{1}{n^2}\,\mathrm{Var}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)$: a constant comes out of a variance squared
$= \tfrac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{Var}(X_i)$: independent draws, so the variances add

hints.text: Start from what $\bar X$ is.
Pull out the $\tfrac{1}{n}$ before splitting the sum.
Definition, then the constant out as $\tfrac{1}{n^2}$, then add the variances, then count them.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $\bar X$ out, take the constant out, then use independence.

byKey.indep: Splitting the variance of the sum needs the sum on its own first. Take the $\tfrac{1}{n}$ out before that.
byKey.end: The count of $n$ variances comes last, once the sum is split.

explain.text: The $\tfrac{1}{n}$ comes out squared, and independence turns the variance of the sum into $n\sigma^2$. So $\mathrm{Var}(\bar X) = \sigma^2 / n$ and the standard error is $\sigma / \sqrt n$. Without independence the variances would not simply add.

screens.title: The sampling distribution of the mean
screens.prose: Every sample gives a different $\bar x$. Across samples, $\bar X$ has $$E[\bar X] = \mu, \qquad \mathrm{SE}(\bar X) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n},$$ and by the central limit theorem its distribution is close to normal once $n$ is moderate. Lesson 9 builds on the standard error.
screens.question: About what share of sample means land within two standard errors of $\mu$?

options.why: 68% is the share within one standard error. Two standard errors catch more.
The normal curve has tails. About 1 sample in 20 lands further out.
Half the means land within about 0.67 standard errors. Two standard errors is much wider.

hints.text: The sampling distribution is close to normal.
A normal puts about 95% of its mass within two sds of its centre.

feedback.correct: About 95%, because $\bar X$ is close to normal.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall the share of a normal within two sds.

explain.text: With $n = 10$, two standard errors is 0.63%. Exactly 95.6% of samples of 10 days land within $0.10\% \pm 0.63\%$; your 1,000 simulated ones gave 96.2%. That is the seed of a confidence interval.

screens.title: A short backtest
screens.prose: A backtest of a new signal shows 20 trades. The average return per trade is 0.4% and the sd of the trade returns is 2.5%. Use 2.5% for $\sigma$.
screens.question: What is the standard error of the average trade return?

hints.text: The question is about the average of 20 trades, not one trade.
Divide the sd of one trade by $\sqrt{20} \approx 4.47$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $s / \sqrt n$ with $n = 20$.

byKey.sd: 2.5% is the spread of single trades. The average of 20 is less noisy: divide by $\sqrt{20}$.
byKey.over-n: You divided by 20. The sd of an average divides by $\sqrt{20}$.

explain.text: The standard error is $2.5\% / \sqrt{20} \approx 0.559\%$. The average, 0.4%, is less than one standard error from zero. A signal with no edge at all would often print a backtest this good.

canvas.caption: Mean 0.4%, standard error 0.56%: within one SE of zero

screens.title: How long a backtest
screens.prose: The researcher wants a standard error of 0.1% per trade, assuming the sd stays at 2.5%. Slide $n$ to explore.
screens.question: How many trades does she need?

hints.text: Solve $2.5 / \sqrt n = 0.1$.
The caption reads 0.100% at the answer.

feedback.correct: 625 trades: over 30 times the backtest she has.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $2.5 / \sqrt n = 0.1$ for $n$.

byKey.no-square: 25 is $\sqrt n$. Square it to get the number of trades.
byKey.linear: You scaled $n$ in line with the error, $20 \times 0.559 / 0.1$. The error shrinks with $\sqrt n$, so square the ratio.

explain.text: $2.5\% / \sqrt{625} = 0.1\%$. Cutting the error by a factor of 5.6 needs $5.6^2 \approx 31$ times the trades. Short backtests are noisy, and the square-root law is why.

ideas: A statistic has a **sampling distribution**: the spread of its values over every sample we might have drawn.
For the sample mean, $E[\bar X] = \mu$ and the sd, the **standard error**, is $\sigma / \sqrt n$; the CLT makes it close to normal.
Halving the standard error takes four times the data. At $n = 1$ the sampling distribution is the population itself.

formula.name: Standard error of the mean
formula.note: Needs independent draws. In practice $\sigma$ is replaced by the sample sd $s$.

summary.trap: The sd of the data is not the sd of the mean. 25 days with sd 1.5% give a mean with standard error 0.3%.

quiz.prose: Daily returns have $\sigma = 2\%$. You average 16 independent days.
quiz.question: What is the standard error of the average? Give a percentage.

byKey.over-n: You divided by 16. The sd of an average divides by $\sqrt{16} = 4$.
byKey.sd: 2% is a single day's spread. The average of 16 days moves less.

explain.text: $\mathrm{SE} = \sigma / \sqrt n = 2\% / 4 = 0.5\%$. The average of 16 days moves a quarter as much as one day.

quiz.prose: An analyst grows her sample from 50 days to 200 days.
quiz.question: What happens to the standard error of her mean?

options.why: You divided by the growth in $n$. The error shrinks with $\sqrt n$, and $\sqrt 4 = 2$.

options.text: It stays the same, since $\sigma$ is the same
options.why: $\sigma$ is the spread of one day; it stays put. The spread of the average falls as $n$ grows.

feedback.correct: Four times the data, half the error.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The standard error is $\sigma / \sqrt n$.

explain.text: $n$ grows by a factor of 4, so $\sqrt n$ grows by 2 and $\sigma / \sqrt n$ halves. The square-root law makes extra precision costly.

quiz.prose: Daily returns have $\mu = 0.1\%$ and $\sigma = 1\%$. Many analysts each average 25 random days.
quiz.question: About 95% of their averages fall in which range?

options.why: You used two sds of a single day. The averages have sd $1\% / 5 = 0.2\%$.
That is one standard error either side, about 68% of averages.
You centred the range on 0. The averages centre on $\mu = 0.1\%$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Centre on $\mu$ and go two standard errors each way.

explain.text: The standard error is $1\% / \sqrt{25} = 0.2\%$. Two of them each side of $\mu = 0.1\%$ gives −0.3% to 0.5%. The sampling distribution is close to normal, so that holds about 95%.
